entries.title: Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
entries.summary: Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists say it began sooner than thought, may have been transmitted from animals to humans and is gaining momentum.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists say it began sooner than thought, may have been transmitted from animals to humans and is gaining momentum.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.

In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.

The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."

Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.

The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.

The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.

The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.

'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister

Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.

Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.

"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.

Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.

Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.

On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."

What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?

Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.

Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.

Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.

Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.

Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.

Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.

Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
entries.summary: A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison

August 11, 2026

A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.

Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials. 

US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia. 

Who is Robert Gilman?

The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance.

He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years.

Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed.

What did Trump and the State Department say about the release?

Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place." 

He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US.

The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard."

The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home."

Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release

Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today."

She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress."

"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"

According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison.

He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said.

Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him.

"It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today."

Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly. 

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?
entries.summary: Turkey’s parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?
entries.content:
Turkey

Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?

August 11, 2026

Turkey’s parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?

One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps.

Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process.

According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms.

PKK law divides society and parliament

Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament.

She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation.

The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives.

Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran. Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors.

According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy.

What's in the law?

The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this.

The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution.

PKK views law as a mere first step

The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either.

They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying.

Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag.

Peace without democratization?

Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP.

For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu. He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption.

The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago.

Criticism of Erdogan's role

Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented.

This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center.

"Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK.

In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process.

Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Hungary's parliament elects Orban critic as new president
entries.summary: Hungary's parliament has overwhelmingly confirmed Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, to the largely ceremonial role of president. New Prime Minister Peter Magyar controversially removed his predecessor.
entries.content:
Hungary

Hungary's parliament elects Orban critic as new president

August 11, 2026

Hungary's parliament has overwhelmingly confirmed Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, to the largely ceremonial role of president. New Prime Minister Peter Magyar controversially removed his predecessor.

Hungary's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday. 

The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections. 

Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure.

Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban, whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role. 

What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote?

The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber.

It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats.

Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment.

Who is Andras Baka?

Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991.

He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court.

In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary.

Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance."

Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious?

Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era.

Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally.

Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end.

Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this "tyrannical" and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory. 

Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president.

What has Baka said about the process and his appointment?

Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat."

However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime.

"There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force."

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: US vaccination executive order: making sense of it
entries.summary: President Donald Trump and his Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

President Donald Trump and his Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context.

US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans." 

The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations.

As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those: 

  • Tuberculosis
  • Hepatitis B
  • Polio
  • Diphtheria
  • Tetanus
  • Pertussis (whooping cough)
  • Haemophilus influenza type B
  • Pneumococcal disease
  • Rotavirus
  • Measles
  • Rubella
  • Human papillomavirus

This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor.

Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas.

Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do.

Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth.

Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list.

This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community.

Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine.

What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say?

Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination.

The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (smallpox).

That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now.

These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe.  Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness.

By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months.

Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time.

This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs.

In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism."

But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general.

Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim.

Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.

The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.

The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines

While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination.

That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again.

This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Allowing bird flu to spread

Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle.

Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well.

On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat
entries.summary: For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.

India's southwest monsoon usually arrives around June, bringing most of the country's annual rainfall, and begins to retreat by September.

Its timing and intensity have always varied, but the broad pattern was predictable enough for farmers, cities and businesses to plan around it. Now, this natural rhythm increasingly seems like a thing of the past.

More than 100 people have been killed across India since late July as heavy monsoon rains triggered floods, landslides and lightning strikes.

The northeastern state of Assam has borne the brunt, with more than 120,000 people affected by flooding. Kerala, Jammu and Kashmir, Bihar and Jharkhand have also reported deaths and widespread disruption.

The problem is not necessarily that India is receiving more rain. It is the way the rain is arriving: longer dry spells are followed by short bursts of intense rainfall that can overwhelm rivers, drainage systems and hillsides.

El Nino has added to this year's variability but scientists say the longer-term changes are being driven by a changing climate.

Have the monsoons entered a new era?

Akshay Deoras, a senior research scientist with the UK's National Centre for Atmospheric Science and the University of Reading, cautions against describing the Indian monsoon as having entered "a fundamentally different regime."

"Active and break spells have always been part of the monsoon. What appears to be changing is their intensity," Deoras told DW.

He pointed out a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, making active spells, or periods of intense rainfall, more intense.

Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Ministry of Earth Sciences, says the change is visible in the behaviour of the monsoon itself.

Average seasonal rainfall, he said, has not shown a systematic long-term change and the monsoon remains a robust natural phenomenon. But the timing, intensity and distribution of rainfall are all noticeably different.

"The characteristics of the Indian monsoon have changed fundamentally," Rajeevan told DW. "We are witnessing an increase in short-duration rainfall extremes, longer dry spells, and changes in the frequency, intensity and distribution of monsoon weather systems."

He believes the rise in extreme rainfall is more than natural variability. "It represents a structural shift in the monsoon system," he said.

Villages and cities both at risk

India's farmers depend heavily on the timing of rainfall. Long dry spells can disrupt sowing and reduce soil moisture and intense rain can wash away fields and damage crops.

India's cities are also struggling due to rapid construction, as new roads and buildings leave less land to absorb water, thus interfering with natural drainage.

Moreover, after weeks of dry weather, hard, dry soil absorbs less water. When heavy rain finally arrives, more of it floods the rivers and drains instead of replenishing groundwater.

India not stepping up to extreme weather hazard

"The greatest risks increasingly come from short periods of very intense rainfall," Deoras told DW, warning that India's infrastructure is increasingly out of step with this changing threat.

Deoras says drainage systems and flood management are still too often designed around historical seasonal rainfall averages rather than the short, high-impact events that cause the greatest disruption.

He noted that forecasting has improved, but knowing that extreme rain is coming is only useful if authorities act on the warning.

Warnings, he said, need to translate into "timely, impact-based decisions" such as changing school schedules, restricting travel or closing off vulnerable areas before heavy rain arrives.

Ritwick Dutta, an environmental lawyer and managing trustee of the Legal Initiative for Forest and Environment, says the problem goes beyond extreme weather itself.

"It is now scientifically accepted that climate change leads to erratic rainfall patterns: high rainfall over a few days followed by long dry periods during the monsoon," Dutta told DW.

"These trends have been compounded by the fact that the decision-making process in India fails to consider climate change while planning construction projects."

Dutta points to the western city of Pune, where a study by the state government and the Energy and Resources Institute projects a 37% increase in rainfall by 2030. Still, Dutta says this projection has not been adequately incorporated into the city's planning, including its riverfront development.

"Dams, embankments and roads are all likely to suffer major damage due to climate change, and yet we proceed as though climate change is a matter to be discussed only in conferences and workshops," Dutta said.

"We are, in effect, 'weaponizing the environment'," Dutta said.

Dutta says India's environmental clearance system does not require climate change to be systematically factored into project decisions.

"The concept of 'climate proofing' does not exist here," he said.

Thousands killed in last year's monsoon

The Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that extreme weather affected India on 331 of 334 monitored days in 2025, or 99% of the period assessed.

More than 4,000 people died, about 3,000 during the monsoon, while at least 30 states and union territories experienced extreme weather simultaneously for eight consecutive months.

Sunita Narain, director general of the CSE, argues that adaptation therefore needs to become part of the country's development strategy.

"Climate change is no longer a future threat. It is already here in the form of extreme heat, extreme rainfall and increasingly destructive weather events," Narain told DW.

"The challenge is no longer proving the science, but redesigning our economy and infrastructure to survive it," she added.

"Cities, roads, drainage systems and water infrastructure can no longer be designed for yesterday's climate."

Every investment, she says, must be planned for a future of more intense and unpredictable weather.

In her reckoning, India must stop treating each flood as an isolated disaster and start planning for a climate in which such extremes are no longer exceptional.

What can be done against extreme weather?

India is facing a whole new pattern of extreme weather. It can record a rainfall deficit nationally while individual regions are underwater. Farmers can go weeks without useful rain and then lose crops in a few hours. Cities can prepare for an average monsoon and still be overwhelmed by one extraordinary downpour.

"The focus now needs to move beyond documenting and discussing these changes towards developing and implementing effective, sector-specific adaptation strategies," climate scientist and former Indian official Rajeevan said.

That means better flood management in cities, changes in agricultural practices, stronger water-storage systems and infrastructure designed around short-duration extreme rainfall rather than historical averages.

India cannot control the monsoon or El Nino and it cannot stop global warming on its own. It can decide, however, where it builds, how it builds and if its new infrastructure is designed for the climate of its future.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing
entries.summary: Thousands remain unaccounted for, with many buried under rubble and rescuers yet to reach more isolated communities. The true scale of the destruction is emerging only slowly, with the death toll likely to rise steeply.
entries.content:
Colombia

Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing

August 11, 2026

Thousands remain unaccounted for, with many buried under rubble and rescuers yet to reach more isolated communities. The true scale of the destruction is emerging only slowly, with the death toll likely to rise steeply.

Rescuers and volunteers searched through collapsed buildings across western Colombia on Tuesday after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread destruction across several major cities a day prior.

The Colombian Association of Capital Cities, known as Asocapitales, put the confirmed death toll at 169 on Tuesday, with 668 people injured.

What do we know about the western Colombia earthquake?

The quake struck near the community of San Jose del Palmar in the western region of Choco on Monday, causing widespread destruction in the cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo and Buenaventura.

Cali accounted for 85 deaths and Pereira 66, according to the association.

The figures remain incomplete because they largely cover major cities and do not yet include the full toll from rural communities.

More than 3,000 people have been reported missing, with many feared trapped beneath collapsed buildings.

Around 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. Soldiers, emergency teams and relatives have been clearing debris in dozens of towns and cities, with volunteers forming lines to pass chunks of concrete by hand.

The cities of Pereira, Cali, Quibdo and Manizales remain on red alert because of the scale of the damage.

At least 165 buildings completely collapsed in those cities alone. Hospitals, airports, public utilities and transport systems have also been damaged across several western departments.

The epicenter was near one of Colombia's poorest and most isolated regions. Large parts of the area can be reached only by boat, aircraft or through jungle routes, while damaged roads and other infrastructure are complicating access. That means the full extent of casualties and destruction near the epicenter remains unclear.

How has the world responded?

The United States has offered $15.5 million (€13.42 million) in emergency assistance, while the European Union has activated its Copernicus satellite service to support rescue operations.

The EU has also begun providing emergency assistance following the earthquake, including €100,000 in initial aid through the German Red Cross.

Israel, Mexico, Chile, Argentina and El Salvador have also offered assistance.

The earthquake was felt beyond Colombia, including in parts of Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.

Why was such a deep quake so damaging?

The scale of the destruction was striking because the earthquake struck at a depth of around 100 kilometers (62 miles), where surface shaking would normally be expected to be weaker.

Geologist Raul Perez of Spain's Geological and Mining Institute told EFE news agency that the magnitude 7.4 quake was a particularly complex subduction event involving the Nazca and South American tectonic plates.

He said a "site effect" in some areas amplified the seismic waves as they passed through local geological formations, increasing both the strength and duration of the shaking and worsening damage to buildings.

Perez said the combination of the quake's unusual depth, its magnitude and the local amplification effects made it an event that would need to be studied closely.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Key issues in Zambia's 2026 general election
entries.summary: Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.
entries.content:
Zambia

Key issues in Zambia's 2026 general election

August 11, 2026

Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.

Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map.

Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents.

His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.

The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women.

Economic issues dominate election campaign

Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising.

"I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo.

Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high."

The government has been making significant gains on these issues.

Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year.

The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances.

Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field

To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate.

There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the ten provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round.

Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties.

Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces.

Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in the densely populated urban districts.

Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.

Can women swing this election?

Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female candidate for president, and four female running mates.

Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat.

"Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates.

Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions.

Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals."

Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said.

Judicial independence called into question

This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary.

In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu.

Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery.

Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission.

"The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW.

Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds.

"These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded.

Amnesty International says Zambian laws including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public.

"The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive.

Continuity or change?

Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms.

The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi.

Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs.

This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration.

This article was compiled from several DW video reports covering Zambia's 2026 general election

entries.title: Afghanistan five years of Taliban rule: Has Germany kept its promises?
entries.summary: After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring all the Afghan local staff members to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
entries.content:
Germany

Afghanistan, the Taliban and German promises

August 11, 2026

After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring all the Afghan local staff members to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June this year, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2500 ($2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Courtruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was cancelled."

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses
entries.summary: The explosion of a Ukrainian decoy drone in Bulgaria near the Romanian border reveals gaps in Bulgaria's defenses, raises questions and shines a light on the country's policy shift on the war in Ukraine.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses

August 11, 2026

The explosion of a Ukrainian decoy drone in Bulgaria near the Romanian border reveals gaps in Bulgaria's defenses, raises questions and shines a light on the country's policy shift on the war in Ukraine.

When a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from.

Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems.

And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged.

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable."

Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident.

What is known about the incident?

At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania.

Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field.

In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives."

Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged.

Drone came down near gas pipeline

The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine, and in close proximity to a Romanian station.

This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target.

Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low.

Wake-up call for Bulgaria

Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability.

"Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT.

While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania, these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach.

Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though he admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country.

"Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one.

With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Was Russia involved?

As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria.

According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated.

Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals.

He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective.

The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication.

Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response

Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash.

"The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case.

As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine.

The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine.

Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador.

"This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position.

A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party.

While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy, promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine.

Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine, blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine.

"I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
